\chapter{Medicine and Keeping Well}
\label{ch:ml-medicine}
\hlchaptermodality{107}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name medicine, treatment and cleanliness, and place them around the symptoms I can already say.}

From cold: three words around falling ill, and which one Malayalam did not have to borrow.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[marunnŭ]{\ml{മരുന്ന്} — medicine}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-marunnu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{fever}. Say \emph{a doctor}. You have had both for a long while, and nothing at all to put between them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} (\emph{marunnŭ}) — \textbf{medicine}.

You can already name what is wrong — the cough, the pain, the tiredness, the fever — and you can name the person you would go to. \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} is the thing that was missing in the middle.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{This one is not borrowed.} It is an old Dravidian word, and Tamil says \emph{marundhu} for the same thing. The remedy has a native name.

That is worth holding on to, because the \textbf{next} word in this chapter — the one for the treatment itself — came from Sanskrit. The substance is named in Malayalam's own words; the practice is named in borrowed ones.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{marunnŭ}
  \item the fever, then the medicine, then the doctor
  \item which language this word comes from, and what Tamil says
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Medicine? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.) Who would you go to for it? (\textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}}.) Is this word borrowed? (\textbf{No} — it is Dravidian, and Tamil has it too.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cikitsa]{\ml{ചികിത്സ} — treatment}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-chikitsa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{medicine}. Say \emph{a doctor}. One of those is a thing; the other is a person. Neither is what happens between them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} (\emph{cikitsa}) — \textbf{treatment}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}} & \emph{vaidyan} & the person \\
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} & \emph{cikitsa} & what the person does \\
\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} & \emph{marunnŭ} & what the person gives \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Sanskrit, where the last word was Dravidian.} That split is ordinary in Malayalam and you have seen it before: the everyday thing keeps its native name, and the formal practice around it takes a borrowed one.

The Sanskrit word has an unusual shape. Its grammarians build it from a root meaning \textbf{to perceive}, in a form that means \textbf{wanting to} — so the word is put together as something like \emph{a wish to see clearly}. Treat that as the traditional account rather than a settled fact; what is certain is the borrowing, not the story inside it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cikitsa}
  \item the three together — \emph{vaidyan}, \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{marunnŭ}
  \item which of the three is the native word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Treatment? (\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}}.) Which of this chapter's two words is borrowed? (\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} — \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} is Dravidian.) Which one is the substance? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vṛtti]{\ml{വൃത്തി} — cleanliness}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-vrtthi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{medicine}, then \emph{treatment}. Both of those come after something has gone wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} (\emph{vṛtti}) — \textbf{cleanliness}.

\textbf{This is the everyday word, and it is worth being plain about its range.} It is what you use about a room, a kitchen, a person's hands. Malayalam has a more formal word for hygiene as a subject — the kind printed on a public notice — and this is not it. This is the one people say.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The Sanskrit it comes from does not mean clean at all.} \emph{vṛtti} is \textbf{conduct} — a way of living, how a person carries themselves.

Malayalam narrowed it. The word for \textbf{how you conduct yourself} became the word for \textbf{how clean you keep things}, which is a short step if you have ever been told that keeping a clean house is a matter of character. Take that as the traditional account of the shift rather than a settled fact; the Sanskrit sense and the Malayalam sense are both well attested, and the road between them is the part that is told rather than proved.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vṛtti}
  \item \emph{marunnŭ}, then \emph{vṛtti} — the cure, and the thing that comes before needing one
  \item what the Sanskrit word behind it meant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Cleanliness? (\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}}.) What did the Sanskrit word behind it mean? (\textbf{Conduct} — a way of living.) Which of this chapter's words is the native one? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\ml{വൃത്തി}, \ml{ചികിത്സ} — on either side of falling ill}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-before-and-after}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{fever}. Say \emph{cough}. Those are the middle of the story.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
Lay this chapter out against what you already had and it makes a line:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} & \emph{vṛtti} & \textbf{before} — keeping well \\
\textbf{\ml{പനി}}, \textbf{\ml{ചുമ}} & \emph{pani}, \emph{cuma} & the thing going wrong \\
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}}, \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} & \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{marunnŭ} & \textbf{after} — getting well \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{You have had the middle of that line for a long while and neither end.} You could say what was wrong and name nobody who would help and nothing that would.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the line in order — \emph{vṛtti}, \emph{pani}, \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{marunnŭ}
  \item which end of it you had first
  \item the person who stands at the far end — \emph{vaidyan}
  \item which one of the four words is not borrowed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word comes \textbf{before} falling ill? (\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}}.) Which two come \textbf{after}? (\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} and \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.) Which of those two is the substance? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[marunnŭ enna ōrmma]{(medicine, treatment, cleanliness) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R107-medicine-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{medicine}, \emph{treatment} and \emph{cleanliness}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one native word among three}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} & \emph{marunnŭ} & \textbf{Dravidian} — Tamil has it too \\
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} & \emph{cikitsa} & Sanskrit \\
\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} & \emph{vṛtti} & Sanskrit, and it meant \textbf{conduct} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The thing you swallow kept its own name; the practice and the virtue came in from Sanskrit.} That is a pattern, not a coincidence, and you saw the same shape in the school words: the building was assembled at home, the scholarly words arrived whole.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You had the symptoms and the person, and nothing in between.} \textbf{\ml{പനി}} and \textbf{\ml{വേദന}} came with the other words for feeling unwell, and \textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}} came with the words for what people do — so you could say what was wrong and who you would see, and not one word about what would actually be done.

Now the line runs end to end: keep clean, fall ill, be treated, take the medicine.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{marunnŭ}, \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{vṛtti}
  \item which one is Dravidian
  \item what \emph{vṛtti} meant in Sanskrit
  \item the whole line, from keeping well to taking the medicine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Medicine, treatment, cleanliness? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}, \ml{ചികിത്സ}, \ml{വൃത്തി}}.) Which one did Malayalam not have to borrow? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.) What did \textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} mean before it meant clean? (\textbf{Conduct}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
